name: David Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, David. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. I'm going to describe five pictures of how AI might change work and ask how you'd react. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, happy to. I'm David, 43, and I'm about eighteen months into carpentry. I was a chef for twenty years, mostly running a kitchen in a restaurant I part-owned, until I sold my share and my back said enough of the night shifts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Before the pictures, tell me about a normal working day for you. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small building cooperative, where the workers own the firm, doing shop and café fit-outs: partitions, counters, shelving, ceilings. I'm on site at seven, and before that I've usually asked an AI app to turn the drawings into a cut list, which saves the gang half an hour of arguing. I like that it's a kitchen without the shouting, everyone with their station, everything to a time. What wears me out is that my hands still don't know what they're doing half the time, and Marek, who's twenty-five, fixes my mitres without saying a word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a relief for most people, and a bit of a letdown for nerds like me. I'd post something like, turns out it's a very good calculator. At the co-op meeting I'd say we should still use what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a little disappointed. I've been using these tools every day, for cut lists, stair maths, even translating safety notes for Marek's cousin who's new. I was half hoping the machines would make me a good carpenter faster than my hands are managing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd keep using the apps for the planning, finish my apprenticeship, and push the co-op to buy a laser scanner so we stop measuring rooms with a tape and a prayer. Money's fine, we've got the restaurant money in savings and Lena's teaching wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, like a party that ended early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'a bit of a letdown'. Isn't it strange to want more disruption?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've already lived through my industry changing. Restaurants went to delivery apps almost overnight and the ones that adapted survived, mine included. Change doesn't frighten me as much as being stuck does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lena think of your AI habit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She teaches science to fifteen-year-olds, and she spends half her life catching kids who let the app write their homework. So she rolls her eyes when I talk to my phone about joists. She also asked me to make her a lesson plan with it last week, so.

S0.say: I'd say it's a relief for most people and a letdown for people like me, and that AI turned out to be a very good calculator. We should still use what works.
S0.think: He'd be a bit disappointed, having hoped AI would speed up his slow progress as a carpenter. He uses the tools daily for planning and translation.
S0.do: Keeps using AI apps for cut lists and planning while finishing his apprenticeship. Pushes the co-op to buy a laser scanner for measuring rooms.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a party ending early.
S0.quote: I was half hoping the machines would make me a good carpenter faster than my hands are managing.
S0.fieldNote: David is the rare person mildly disappointed by the calm picture, because he hoped AI would make up for his slow hands. His past as a restaurant owner who survived the delivery-app shift shapes his comfort with change. Money isn't a worry for him here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is why I work in a co-op: when the machines come, the workers decide what to do with the time they save. I'd say every firm should be run like that. And I'd say the government should pay for retraining, because not everyone has a restaurant to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. I'm a weak carpenter but a strong planner, and if the tools take more of the cutting and measuring, then the person who knows how to run them is worth more. I'm the worst on the gang with a chisel and the best with the software, so this is the picture where I catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy a layout robot myself, one of those little machines that drives around the floor marking where the walls go, maybe a few thousand out of savings. I'd offer it to the co-op and run it on our jobs. On weekends I'd start doing small café counters for people I know from my kitchen days, designed with the AI and cut properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and, honestly, a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tony, who's 58 and has never sent a text with a photo in it. He's the best hand-joiner I've met. I'd want the co-op to keep him on the bits machines are bad at, the old shopfronts, the curved stuff, and I'd make sure he gets the credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're spending your own savings on a robot. Isn't that risky for a family with a mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a few months' worth, not the house. We've got well over a year put by, and I spent twenty years gambling on whether people would like my risotto. A robot that marks floors is less of a gamble than a new menu.

S1.say: I'd say this is why co-ops matter, because workers decide what to do with the time machines save. Government should pay for retraining because most people have nothing to fall back on.
S1.think: He thinks it's good for him because he's a weak carpenter but strong with software. This is the picture where he catches up with the rest of the gang.
S1.do: Buys a layout robot with a few thousand from savings and runs it on co-op jobs. Starts doing small café counters at weekends for contacts from his chef days, designed with AI.
S1.quote: I'm the worst on the gang with a chisel and the best with the software, so this is the picture where I catch up.
S1.fieldNote: David sees steady disruption as his chance to turn software skill into standing on site. He spends his own savings on kit, calling it smaller than a restaurant gamble. He thinks quickly about protecting Tony, an older hand-joiner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to make sure workers own the robots, not just a few billionaires. I'd be at the co-op federation meetings, I'd be online arguing for public ownership of the big models. I'd say it loudly: if it can do any job, then the gains belong to everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think two years is too fast even for me. I like change, but I can't learn faster than a machine that learns everything at once. Money-wise we'd be fine for a while, but I'd be 45 with no trade that anyone needs, again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd put a big chunk of the savings into paying the mortgage down, so the house is safe whatever happens. I'd push the co-op to buy robots ourselves so we're the ones renting them out, not the ones being replaced. And I'd go to every meeting and vote for whoever wants to tax the AI firms properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Wired and a bit sick, like the night before opening a restaurant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't much warning. What changes for you between now and 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, there's no point training as something new, because by the time I'm qualified the machine is too. So the time goes on money and on the co-op: getting the house safer and getting us owning the kit. It's less a plan than grabbing what you can before the doors shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're someone who likes change. Why is this one different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every other change I've seen left a gap for people to move into. When delivery apps came, I moved into catering for offices. If the machine can do every job, there's no gap to run to, just a question of who gets the money.

S2.say: I'd say workers must own the robots, not just billionaires, and push for public ownership of the big AI models. If it can do any job, the gains belong to everyone.
S2.think: He thinks two years is too fast even for someone who loves change, because he can't out-learn a machine that learns everything. Money would hold for a while, but he'd be left with no trade anyone needs.
S2.do: Puts a big chunk of savings into paying down the mortgage straight away. Pushes the co-op to buy and rent out robots itself, and votes for whoever will tax AI firms properly.
S2.feel: Anxious, wired and a bit sick, like the night before a restaurant opening.
S2.quote: I can't learn faster than a machine that learns everything at once.
S2.fieldNote: This is where David's love of change runs out: he sees no gap to move into when a machine can do every job. His answer is ownership, both of his house and through the co-op owning robots. He doesn't spin it as a plan, calling it grabbing what you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for workers to get organised and own a piece of this. I'd be pushing every co-op I know to start buying and learning the robots now. Online I'd say, stop fearing it and start owning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a different game for me. I'd have my ticket, I'd know the machines inside out, and I could be the person who programmes the site robots and checks their work. With two years I'm a passenger. With five, I'm the one holding the remote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd sign up for whatever robot-operator course exists, even if it's a bit rubbish at first, and keep doing my apprenticeship alongside. I'd put maybe a fifth of our savings into the co-op's robot fund. When it lands, I'd want to be running a small team of machines on fit-outs, with Marek and Tony doing the fine work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years actually change, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes whether I'm early or late. In two years everyone's late, even the companies. In five years, the people who started now are the ones the firms come to, and I want to be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Sasha and Ivy? Would you talk to them about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sasha's eleven and already better with the apps than me, so I'd teach her to use them for making things, not just watching videos. Ivy's eight, she just wants to bake with me. I'd keep cooking with her, because I think the things you do with your hands for people you love won't go anywhere.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for workers to organise and own a piece of this, and every co-op should start buying and learning robots now. Stop fearing it and start owning it.
S3.think: He thinks five years lets him become the person who programmes the site robots and checks their work. He moves from passenger to the one holding the remote.
S3.do: Signs up for a robot-operator course in year one while finishing his apprenticeship. Puts about a fifth of savings into the co-op's robot fund and aims to run a small team of machines on fit-outs.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more curious than scared.
S3.quote: With two years I'm a passenger. With five, I'm the one holding the remote.
S3.fieldNote: For David the timing is about being early rather than late, and five years makes him early. He'd put real money into the co-op's robots. His instinct to keep baking with his youngest shows what he thinks will last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this fairly, with shorter weeks and workers owning the machines. I'd say we've wasted chances before, so let's not waste this one. I'd be the one at the co-op meeting with a ten-year plan on a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd quite like this one. Ten years is time to get good at carpentry, then become the robot guy, then maybe set up something of my own. I've already reinvented myself once at forty. Twice by fifty-three sounds about right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship properly first, because I'd like to actually be a carpenter for a few years. Then around year three or four I'd train on the machines and help the co-op buy its first proper fleet. I'd keep the savings as they are and maybe open a small food stall on weekends, just for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit cheerful, which I know isn't how most people would feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why finish the apprenticeship if machines will do the work by 2036 anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because you can't check a robot's joint if you've never made one. My chefs who'd never cooked by hand were useless at spotting when the oven was wrong. Knowing the craft is how you know when the machine's lying to you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment you picture, in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I picture the co-op's yard with four or five machines lined up, and Tony, retired, coming by on a Friday to tell us they're all doing it wrong. I'd want there to still be a Friday where people come by and tell you you're doing it wrong.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this fairly, with shorter weeks and workers owning the machines. We've wasted chances before and shouldn't waste this one.
S4.think: He'd quite like this picture, with time to master carpentry, then robots, then perhaps his own business. He's reinvented himself once at forty and thinks twice by fifty-three sounds right.
S4.do: Finishes his apprenticeship properly, then trains on machines around year three or four and helps the co-op buy its first fleet. Keeps savings as they are and maybe opens a weekend food stall for fun.
S4.feel: Calm and even cheerful, knowing most people wouldn't feel that way.
S4.quote: I'd want there to still be a Friday where people come by and tell you you're doing it wrong.
S4.fieldNote: David is most at ease with a decade, which suits his habit of reinventing himself. He insists on learning the craft first, comparing it to chefs who can't tell when the oven's wrong. His picture of 2036 is about people, not machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because nobody gets to be early, and the gains go to whoever already owns everything. What would help is rules that let workers and co-ops own a share of the machines, and public money to help small firms buy them. A basic income for people who can't adapt, too, because not everyone has a restaurant to sell.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss Marek fixing my mitres without saying anything. That little bit of being taught by someone younger than you, I don't know how a machine replaces that.

headlineQuote: I've already reinvented myself once at forty. Twice by fifty-three sounds about right.
portrait: David Petrov is a 43-year-old former chef and restaurant part-owner who sold his share and is now about eighteen months into carpentry with a worker-owned fit-out co-op. He's a weak hand with a chisel but uses AI every day for cut lists and planning, and he likes change more than most. His progressive answer to every picture is for workers and co-ops to own the machines. He stays calm through the plateau and steady change, becomes anxious at AGI in two years because there's no gap left to move into, and grows calmer and even cheerful as the warning time stretches to ten years.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because nobody gets the chance to be early and the gains go to those who already own everything.
whatWouldHelp: Rules and public money that let workers and co-ops own a share of the machines, and a basic income for people who can't adapt.
